cards.title: Scams in your pocket
cards.body:
The same tricks as [[phishing]] emails also arrive as **text messages** and **phone calls**. Texts are short and urgent, and a phone ringing makes people act fast.

Knowing the patterns takes the pressure off.

cards.title: Scam texts
cards.body:
Common scam texts say you owe a **parcel fee** or a **road toll**, that you've won something, or "Hi Mum, this is my new number".

Sender names can be faked, so a scam text can even land **in the same thread** as real messages from that company.

Warning signs: a **small fee** to pay, a **deadline**, and an **unfamiliar link**. Real companies let you check in their **official app or website**, so go there instead of tapping the link.

cards.prompt: Tap the **three** warning signs in the **new** message.
cards.explanation: The new message asks for a **small fee**, sets a **deadline**, and links to `parcels-redelivery.example`, an **unfamiliar link**. The older message and the sender name look normal, which is exactly how these scams blend in.
cards.hint: Only look at the new message. Which parts match the warning signs: a fee, a deadline and a link?
cards.nudge: Three parts of the new message match the warning signs for texts. Go through those signs one at a time.

cards.title: Scam calls and cloned voices
cards.body:
Scam callers pretend to be your bank, the government, tech support or even the police. They may ask for a **sign-in code**, your **password**, to **control your computer**, or for payment in **gift cards**.

Computers can now **copy a voice** from a short clip, so a call can sound just like someone you know.

Two simple defences:
- **Hang up and call back** on a number you already know: your contact list, or the one on the official website.
- Agree a **family safe word**, one that isn't posted anywhere, to ask for in an emergency.

Being told to **keep it secret** or to **stay on the line** is a warning sign too.

cards.prompt: Your phone rings. It sounds exactly like your cousin.

steps.text: **"It's me! I'm in trouble and need $200 in gift cards right now. Don't tell anyone!"** What do you do?

choices.text: Buy the gift cards. It's their voice
choices.consequence: Voices can be copied, and gift cards are a favourite scam payment. The money would be gone.

choices.text: Keep it secret, like they asked
choices.consequence: Secrecy is a warning sign. It stops anyone helping you check.

choices.text: Hang up and call your cousin on their saved number
choices.consequence: Your cousin answers, confused, and fine. It was a scam, and you stopped it.

cards.explanation: A familiar voice can be faked. **Hang up and call back** on a number you already know, or ask for your family safe word. Secrecy and gift cards are warning signs.
cards.hint: Remember the two defences for calls. And what did the lesson say about keeping secrets and gift cards?

items.label: Caller asks for the code texted to you
Caller wants to control your computer
"Pay in gift cards or be arrested"
Caller says to keep it from your family
You call the number on the bank's site
You call a friend on their saved number

cards.explanation: Asking for codes, remote control of your computer, gift-card payments and secrecy are all scam signs: **hang up**. Calling a number you found yourself, or a friend on their saved number, is fine.
cards.hint: Check each against the warning signs for calls: codes, controlling your computer, gift cards, secrecy. Who made the call, and with what number?
cards.nudge: Check each against the warning signs for calls. It also matters who made the call, and to what number.

cards.title: Too good to be true
cards.body:
Some scams offer something amazing: a prize you never entered, a free phone, "double your money", **free game coins or skins**, or a job paying lots for very little work.

Watch for **paying a fee to get a prize**, and for payment by **gift cards**, crypto or a money-transfer app. Real prizes don't cost money to claim.

cards.prompt: Which of these is **always** a warning sign?

options.text: Paying a fee with gift cards to claim a prize
An email receipt for something you just bought
options.nudge: A receipt for something you really bought is normal. Look for a request that real companies never make.

options.text: A text from your school about an excursion
options.nudge: Schools do send reminders. Look for the one that asks you to pay for a prize.

cards.explanation: Real prizes never cost money to claim, and gift cards are a favourite way for scammers to be paid. A receipt or a school reminder can be perfectly normal.
cards.hint: Think about what the lesson said about prizes and ways of paying.

cards.prompt: A website promises **10,000 free coins** for your favourite game.

steps.text: It asks for your **game username and password** to "send the coins". What do you do?

choices.consequence: The site keeps your password and takes over your account. There were never any coins.

choices.text: Close the page. Coins only come from the game itself
choices.consequence: Your account stays yours. Free-coin generators are a common trick to steal accounts.

cards.explanation: "Free coins" sites are **too good to be true**. Never type your game password anywhere except the game's own app or website.
cards.hint: Is this too good to be true? And who should ever see your password?

cards.prompt: Label the three warning signs in the new message.
cards.explanation: The **small fee** and the **deadline** are the pressure. The **unfamiliar link** is where they want you to go.
cards.hint: Match each label to one part of the new message: what it wants paid, how long you have, and where it sends you.
cards.nudge: Each label is one of the three warning signs for texts. Take one at a time and find the line that shows it.

cards.title: Recap
cards.body:
- Scam texts use a **small fee**, a **deadline** and an **unfamiliar link**. Check in the official app instead.
- Scam calls can use a **copied voice**. **Hang up and call back** on a number you know, and use a family safe word.
- Codes, remote control, gift cards and secrecy are **warning signs**.
- **Too good to be true** usually is.

Next: websites that are copies of the real thing.
